candidates.title: Unbounded Delegation Chain Depth with No Cycle Detection Enables Infinite Auth Loops and Resource Exhaustion in Multi-Agent Topologies
candidates.attack_scenario: The A2A protocol explicitly enables multi-hop authorization delegation chains via TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED (section 7.6), stating this 'enables forming a chain of Tasks in TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED.' However, the protocol defines no maximum delegation depth counter, no chain identifier, and no cycle detection mechanism. In a topology where Agent A delegates to Agent B, Agent B delegates to Agent C, and Agent C's auth request ultimately routes back to Agent A (directly or through additional hops), a circular delegation loop forms. Each agent individually follows the protocol correctly: receiving an AUTH_REQUIRED state and propagating it upstream via the authorization_delegation transition, whose guard checks only client.is_a2a_agent and client.is_actively_processing_task — no guard checks for chain depth or prior participation. Each hop holds server-side resources (the task in AUTH_REQUIRED, any open stream). The cycle continues indefinitely because no agent has visibility into the full chain topology — the protocol's hop-by-hop interaction model (confirmed as a gap in F-002) means each agent sees only its immediate caller. Even without malicious intent, a mesh topology of cooperative agents can accidentally form cycles. Research confirms 'delegation depth violation' is an attack category in multi-agent systems that requires explicit protocol-level mitigation.

SSE stream is established. Task begins processing. Stream will remain open for the task's entire duration.
Stream becomes active. Server sends events. Protocol defines no periodic re-authentication heartbeat, no auth-challenge event type, no credential refresh mechanism.

Hours pass. The original auth token has expired or been revoked (user deactivated, session terminated by admin, token blacklisted). Server continues sending status updates and artifact data on the stream because no protocol mechanism signals credential invalidation mid-stream.

Potentially sensitive task output continues flowing to the client whose authorization has been revoked. The client receives data it should no longer have access to. The protocol defines no STREAM_AUTH_EXPIRED event type and no mandatory stream termination on credential lifecycle events.

involved_states.relevance: The stream remains in ACTIVE state indefinitely with no protocol mechanism to transition based on credential lifecycle events. The only exit transitions are task state changes, not auth state changes.
Stream closure is triggered only by task reaching terminal/interrupted state. No auth-related closure trigger exists in the protocol.

involved_transitions.relevance: This self-loop continues regardless of credential validity. Guard checks stream.state = STREAM_ACTIVE, not credential.valid = true.
The ONLY protocol-defined exit from STREAM_ACTIVE. Trigger is task state change, not credential expiry. No 'credential_expired' or 'auth_revoked' trigger exists.

candidates.missing_primitive: A protocol-level credential lifecycle management mechanism for long-lived streams: either a mandatory periodic re-authentication heartbeat event that the server sends and the client must respond to with fresh credentials, an AUTH_CHALLENGE stream event type that signals credential expiry and allows in-band re-authentication, a protocol-defined maximum stream duration tied to credential lifetime with mandatory resubscription, or a STREAM_AUTH_EXPIRED event type that the server sends when it detects credential revocation, signaling the client to obtain fresh credentials before resubscribing.
candidates.why_compliance_does_not_prevent: The server fully complied by authenticating the initial HTTP request. The protocol's 'MUST authenticate every incoming request' was satisfied — the SSE stream IS one request, authenticated at establishment. No normative rule requires mid-stream credential re-validation, periodic re-authentication, or stream termination on credential lifecycle events. The protocol defines task-state-based stream closure but no auth-state-based stream closure. A fully compliant server with short-lived tokens faces an irreconcilable tension between the protocol's single-request-auth model and the multi-hour stream duration it supports.

structural_observations: The FSM has no transition from TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED or TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED to TASK_STATE_FAILED. The only exits from interrupted states are: client provides input/credentials (→ WORKING) or cancel (→ CANCELED). A server-initiated timeout from an interrupted state to FAILED would require a transition not currently present in the protocol's state machine, meaning the protocol structurally prevents servers from timing out stuck interrupted tasks without canceling them.

The PushNotificationConfig.authentication field is optional in both the TypeScript type definition (authentication?: PushNotificationAuthenticationInfo) and the protobuf definition (AuthenticationInfo authentication = 4 without REQUIRED annotation). The normative MUST for server-to-webhook authentication is conditional on this field being present: 'The A2A Server MUST authenticate itself to the client's webhook URL according to the scheme specified in PushNotificationConfig.authentication.' When omitted, the protocol permits unauthenticated push notifications, creating a tension with the non-normative guidance that webhook endpoints 'MUST rigorously verify the authenticity of incoming notification requests.'

The protocol's version negotiation has a backward-compatibility provision: 'except for 0.3 Clients - 0.3 will be assumed for empty header.' This means servers that support both v0.3 and v1.0 will interpret missing A2A-Version headers as v0.3 requests. Since v1.0 modernized OAuth flows (removing implicit/password grants), this creates a theoretical downgrade surface, though it is mitigated by the fundamental assumption that compliant v1.0 clients MUST send the header.

The referenceTaskIds field in the Message data model enables cross-task references but inherits the same authorization gap identified in F-004 (task-to-identity binding). A client referencing another client's task ID has no protocol-level authorization check beyond the general 'appropriate authorization scoping' MUST, which lacks a defined mechanism.
